definition: Subsidize means to support with money; to pay part of the cost of something.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word subsidize. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know subsidize should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: For a century the crown subsidized the royal glassworks, buying half its coal so the furnaces never went cold.
Chipping in is much lighter than subsidizing: a few dollars toward the office gift is chipping in, while subsidizing means steadily paying a real share of something's cost.
Bankroll goes further than subsidize — a subsidized clinic still bills for part of each visit, while a bankrolled one has its every cost carried by someone else.

To fund something, said plainly, is to be the money behind it — a funded lab expects every bill covered. Subsidize claims less on purpose: it means paying part of the cost, a share alongside what the farmer, rider, or patient still pays. The part is the point.

To underwrite something is to promise in advance to absorb its cost or risk so others can safely proceed — the underwriter stands behind possible losses that may never arrive. Subsidize is steadier and plainer: actually paying part of an ongoing bill, season after season, as standing policy.

A family that resides on Elm Street sits there day after day — the same sedere, settled instead of standing behind.
Subsidize means to support with money; to pay part of the cost of something.
Day boats were losing the ice war: the big trawlers had freezer holds, and the co-op's icehouse charged what ice costs.
So the port council now subsidizes every small boat's ice, paying forty percent of the bill straight from the town's accounts.
The fleet did not get richer — it got possible.

Subsidize is the exact word for what the council does, because subsidize means to support with money — to pay part of the cost of something — and the part matters: the boats still buy their ice, just not alone.
Donate would be a one-time gift; a subsidy is scheduled money with a policy behind it.
Subsidize is budget language: governments, councils, and endowments subsidize fares, lunches, and clinics — ongoing, partial, on purpose.
Its unit-mates give differently: a benefactor gives as a person, and largess and munificence describe gifts, not line items.
If the support recurs and covers part of a price, subsidize is the precise word.

When the city pool raised its lesson fees, the council faced a choice.
Some members wanted the city to take over the swim program's budget entirely; others wanted to do nothing at all.
The compromise that passed did neither.
The city would subsidize lessons for any child under eighteen: families kept paying, but the city quietly covered forty percent of every bill.
The program's director liked the arrangement more than a full takeover.
Parents who paid something, she argued, showed up more; a city that paid something, she noticed, asked fewer questions than one that paid everything.
Ten years on, the ledger shows the same steady split — the families' share and the city's share, side by side, every term.
